docs.t: Mechanic and pink slips in Warwick Farm: What's that light on your dash?
docs.a: Tap a light to see what it means and whether to keep driving. How to read a warning light. Choose a light to see what it usually means. Amber light: get it checked soon. Check engine. What it usually means. The engine computer has found a fault. It can be small, like a loose fuel cap, or something that needs fixing, like a sensor or ignition problem. Can I keep driving? If it stays on steadily, you can usually drive on gently and book it in soon. If it flashes, the engine may be misfiring badly: slow down, stop somewhere safe as soon as you can and call, as driving on can damage the exhaust system. Your owner's manual has the details for your car. Red light: act now. Battery or charging. What it usually means. The battery isn't being charged. Common causes are a worn alternator, a loose or broken drive belt, or a battery or wiring fault. Can I keep driving? Not far. The car is running on what's left in the battery and may stop. Switch off what you don't need, like the air con and radio, and get somewhere safe. If other lights come on too, stop. Red light: stop safely. Oil pressure. What it usually means. Oil pressure is too low. The engine may be low on oil, or there may be a fault with the oil pump or a sensor. Can I keep driving? No. Stop as soon as it's safe and switch the engine off. An engine without oil pressure can be damaged quickly. Check the oil level once it has cooled, and call before driving on. Red light: stop safely. Brake system. What it usually means. On most cars it lights up when the park brake is on. If it stays on with the park brake off, the brake fluid may be low or there may be a fault in the brakes. Can I keep driving? Check the park brake first. If the light stays on, stop somewhere safe and don't drive on until the brakes have been checked. Amber light: get it checked soon. ABS. What it usually means. The anti-lock braking system has a fault. Your normal brakes should still work, but the wheels can lock under hard braking. Can I keep driving? Usually yes, carefully. Leave extra room in front and book it in soon. If the red brake light is on as well, stop safely. Amber light: get it checked soon. Tyre pressure. What it usually means. One or more tyres is below its set pressure. Only cars with tyre pressure monitoring have this light. Can I keep driving? Gently, to the nearest air pump. Inflate the tyres to the pressures on the tyre placard, often inside the driver's door. If a tyre looks flat or the car pulls to one side, stop somewhere safe. Red on many cars: don't put it off. Airbag (SRS). What it usually means. The airbag system has found a fault. The airbags, and on some cars the seatbelt pretensioners, may not work in a crash. Can I keep driving? The car will usually drive normally, but you and your passengers are less protected. Have it checked soon. Red light: stop safely. Engine temperature. What it usually means. The engine is running too hot. Common causes are low coolant, a leak, or a fault with the fan, thermostat or water pump. Can I keep driving? No. Stop as soon as it's safe and switch off. Let the engine cool, and never open the radiator cap while it's hot. Call before driving on. Something you notice, not a warning light. Air con not cooling. What it usually means. The system may be low on gas from a slow leak, or a part such as the compressor or a fan may have a fault. Can I keep driving? Yes. The air con also helps clear a fogged windscreen, so take more care in wet weather until it's fixed. docs.a: What the check engine, oil, battery, brake, ABS and temperature lights usually mean, and whether you can keep driving. General guidance from a mechanic. AI illustration AI illustration, not a photo of our workshop.  This is general guidance only.  Cars differ, so check your owner's manual for what each light means on your car.  If a light comes on with a noise, smell, smoke or the car feels different, pull over somewhere safe and call.

docs.t: Car warning lights: what they mean: Red or amber: how to read the colour
docs.a: Red usually means stop when it's safe, or act now. Amber usually means get it checked soon. Most lights also flash on for a moment when you start the car. That's the car checking its own bulbs and systems. It's only a warning if the light stays on, comes back on while driving, or flashes.

docs.t: Car warning lights: what they mean: The lights you'll see most often
docs.a: Check engine light. Amber light: get it checked soon. What it usually means. The engine computer has found a fault. It can be small, like a loose fuel cap, or something that needs fixing, like a sensor or ignition problem. Can I keep driving? If it stays on steadily, you can usually drive on gently and book it in soon. If it flashes, the engine may be misfiring badly: slow down, stop somewhere safe as soon as you can and call, as driving on can damage the exhaust system. Your owner's manual has the details for your car. Oil pressure light. Red light: stop safely. What it usually means. Oil pressure is too low. The engine may be low on oil, or there may be a fault with the oil pump or a sensor. Can I keep driving? No. Stop as soon as it's safe and switch the engine off. An engine without oil pressure can be damaged quickly. Check the oil level once it has cooled, and call before driving on. Battery or charging light. Red light: act now. What it usually means. The battery isn't being charged. Common causes are a worn alternator, a loose or broken drive belt, or a battery or wiring fault. Can I keep driving? Not far. The car is running on what's left in the battery and may stop. Switch off what you don't need, like the air con and radio, and get somewhere safe. If other lights come on too, stop. Brake system light. Red light: stop safely. What it usually means. On most cars it lights up when the park brake is on. If it stays on with the park brake off, the brake fluid may be low or there may be a fault in the brakes. Can I keep driving? Check the park brake first. If the light stays on, stop somewhere safe and don't drive on until the brakes have been checked. ABS light. Amber light: get it checked soon. What it usually means. The anti-lock braking system has a fault. Your normal brakes should still work, but the wheels can lock under hard braking. Can I keep driving? Usually yes, carefully. Leave extra room in front and book it in soon. If the red brake light is on as well, stop safely. Engine temperature light. Red light: stop safely. What it usually means. The engine is running too hot. Common causes are low coolant, a leak, or a fault with the fan, thermostat or water pump. Can I keep driving? No. Stop as soon as it's safe and switch off. Let the engine cool, and never open the radiator cap while it's hot. Call before driving on. Tyre pressure light. Amber light: get it checked soon. What it usually means. One or more tyres is below its set pressure. Only cars with tyre pressure monitoring have this light. Can I keep driving? Gently, to the nearest air pump. Inflate the tyres to the pressures on the tyre placard, often inside the driver's door. If a tyre looks flat or the car pulls to one side, stop somewhere safe. Airbag (SRS) light. Red on many cars: don't put it off. What it usually means. The airbag system has found a fault. The airbags, and on some cars the seatbelt pretensioners, may not work in a crash. Can I keep driving? The car will usually drive normally, but you and your passengers are less protected. Have it checked soon.

docs.t: Car warning lights: what they mean: What to do when a light comes on
docs.a: Note the colour and whether it's steady or flashing. Red or flashing means find somewhere safe to stop. Notice how the car feels. Any new noise, smell, smoke, loss of power or change in the brakes or steering means stop. Check the simple things once you're stopped. The park brake for the brake light, the oil level once the engine has cooled, the fuel cap for a check engine light. Look it up in the owner's manual , which shows every light for your model. Call before driving on if it's a red light or you're unsure. Describe what the light is doing and we'll tell you what to do next.

docs.a: Some lights matter at rego time too. If one of these has been on for a while, get it fixed before your pink slip . You can tap through each light on the warning lights panel on our home page , or see the repairs we handle at Shine .

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is
docs.a: What a logbook service is, what AI illustration AI illustration, not a photo of our workshop.  Quick answer Your car's maker lists what should be done at each service and when, usually every so many kilometres or months.  A logbook service follows that list for your car's interval, and the service is recorded in the logbook so there's a history of the work.

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is: What the logbook is
docs.a: Most cars come with a service logbook, either a printed book in the glovebox or an online record. It sets out the service schedule for your model: what's done at each interval and the distance or time each one falls due. The schedule is written for your exact car. A small petrol hatch and a turbo-diesel ute have very different lists, so there's no single "standard service". That's the point of following the logbook rather than a generic oil change.

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is: What's usually included
docs.a: It depends on the interval, but a logbook service usually includes some of these: engine oil and oil filter change, with the grade the maker specifies. checking and topping up fluids, such as coolant, brake fluid and washer fluid. air filter, cabin filter and fuel filter, at the intervals listed. a check of the brakes, tyres, steering, suspension, lights, wipers and battery. bigger scheduled items at certain intervals, such as spark plugs, brake fluid replacement, coolant replacement or a timing belt. a record of the service in the logbook and, where the car has one, the service reminder reset. If the inspection finds something outside the schedule, like worn brake pads or a leaking shock absorber, ask the workshop to tell you what it found, what it costs and how urgent it is before any extra work is done.

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is: How to tell when your service is due
docs.a: A service reminder on the dash, often a spanner symbol or a message. The windscreen sticker from your last service, showing the date or distance for the next one. The logbook itself . Find the last stamped entry and look up the next interval. Most schedules say "whichever comes first". If you don't drive much, the time limit can come up well before the kilometres. Oil and fluids age even when the car is parked.

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is: Why it matters
docs.a: It catches wear early. Each service includes a look over the car. Worn tyres, a weeping water pump or a perished drive belt are cheaper to fix when they're found on the hoist than when they let go on the M5. It keeps the big jobs on time. Some parts, like timing belts on engines that have them, are replaced at set intervals in the schedule. Missing one can mean serious engine damage. The logbook is how you know it's due. It builds a service history. A full, stamped logbook shows the next owner the car has been looked after. Buyers ask about it, and it can make a car easier to sell. It helps at rego time. A car that's serviced on time is less likely to fail its pink slip on brakes, tyres, wipers or leaks, because those get looked at along the way.

Bring your logbook, or the details of your online one, so we can follow your car's schedule and record the service. If a warning light has come on since your last service, tell us when you book. Our guide to dashboard warning lights explains which ones mean stop. You can also see everything we do at Shine .

docs.t: Logbook servicing: what it is: Common questions
docs.a: What is a logbook service? How often do I need a logbook service? It depends on your car. The logbook gives each interval as a distance or a time, whichever comes first. Check the last stamped entry or your windscreen sticker. docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW
docs.a: What AI illustration AI illustration, not a photo of our workshop.  Quick answer Diesel: the same pink slip as a petrol car.  Brakes, steering, tyres, lights, body and leaks, including leaks from the fuel system.  LPG: the standard pink slip plus a gas system check by an examiner authorised for gas vehicles.  Tell the station your car runs on LPG when you book.

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: Who can do an LPG pink slip
docs.a: Not every inspector can check a gas car. In NSW, examiners first need their standard Authorised Inspection Scheme accreditation. To inspect gas-powered vehicles, they then complete extra training under the Authorised Gas Inspection Scheme, and Transport for NSW adds LPG and CNG to their record. So when you ring around for an LPG pink slip, ask whether the station can do gas cars. Shine does pink slips for petrol, diesel and LPG vehicles.

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: What's checked on an LPG car
docs.a: The NSW safety check standards have a whole section for LPG and CNG fuel systems. In plain English, the examiner looks at: The LPG compliance plate. The gas installation must have an approved compliance plate showing it meets the Australian standard. For current installations that's AS/NZS 1425. The plate should reflect the most recent installation, repair or change to the system. The number plate labels. LPG cars must show an LPG label on the front and rear number plates: white lettering on a red background. On systems installed since 1 October 1999, it sits on a small metal diamond plate. The tank. It must be securely mounted so it can't be removed without tools, and free of advanced corrosion, fire damage, deep dents or cuts. Mounting straps can't be cut or badly rusted. The tank's service life. An LPG tank must be checked for continued service life every ten years. If its statutory life has expired, the car fails. Gas leaks. The examiner applies a foaming solution or uses a gas detector on the fuel lines, joints and components. Any leak fails the check. Valves and fittings. The fuel selector and other parts must be securely mounted, and the pressure relief valve must be fitted so any discharge wouldn't strike the exhaust or a bystander. All the normal pink slip items still apply on top of this: brakes, tyres, lights and the rest of our pink slip checklist .

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: LPG systems fitted interstate
docs.a: If the gas system was installed in another state or territory, NSW can still accept it. It needs a metal plate near the installation showing it complies with the Australian standard, the date it was commissioned, where it was installed, the installer's number, the VIN and the tank's serial number. It also has to pass a safety check by an examiner authorised for gas vehicles. A car coming in from interstate needs a blue slip rather than a pink slip to be registered here. See pink slip vs blue slip .

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: Diesel pink slips
docs.a: A diesel car or ute gets the same safety check as a petrol one. There's no separate diesel test in the light vehicle standards. The parts that tend to matter more on diesels are the ones that wear with work: Fuel leaks. Any leak from the fuel system fails the check, so look for wet patches around the injector lines, filter and tank. Oil leaks. Oil from the engine, gearbox or driveline dripping onto the road, exhaust or brakes is a reason to fail. Exhaust. It must be securely mounted and not leaking. Tyres and suspension on utes and four-wheel drives that tow or carry loads. A towbar, if fitted, is checked too.

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: Fees for LPG and diesel cars
docs.a: The NSW fees page lists maximum fees by vehicle type, not by fuel. For a light vehicle from 1 July 2026, the maximum is $52 for a pink slip and $82 for a blue slip, including GST. If the car fails and you have it repaired and rechecked at the same station within 14 days, there's no second inspection fee.

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: Avoiding a second trip
docs.a: Find the LPG compliance plate and make sure the number plate labels are on and readable. If you smell gas, don't wait for the pink slip. Have it checked now. If the tank is getting close to ten years since it was last certified, ask us about it when you book. For diesels, have any leaks looked at during a service first. For the current fees in one place, see the pink and blue slip section on our home page .

docs.t: LPG and diesel pink slips in NSW: Common questions
docs.a: Can any inspection station do an LPG pink slip? No. The examiner must be authorised to inspect gas-powered vehicles under the Authorised Gas Inspection Scheme. Ask when you book. How often does an LPG tank need to be recertified? The NSW safety check standards say an LPG tank must be checked for continued service life every ten years. A tank past its statutory life fails the check. Is a diesel pink slip different from a petrol one? No. Diesels get the same light vehicle safety check. Fuel leaks, oil leaks and exhaust condition are checked on both. Does an LPG pink slip cost more? The NSW fees page sets maximum fees by vehicle type, not fuel. For a light vehicle the maximum pink slip fee is $52 from 1 July 2026.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked
docs.a: What a NSW pink slip (safety check) looks at: brakes, tyres, steering, lights, windscreen, seatbelts, rust and leaks, and the faults that commonly fail. AI illustration AI illustration, not a photo of our workshop.  Examiners work from Transport for NSW's Light Vehicle Safety Check Standards, part of the Authorised Inspection Scheme (AIS) rules.  You may also see the pink slip called an eSafety check.  Below is what those standards cover for a car, ute or light four-wheel drive, written the way we'd explain it at the counter.  Quick answer The check covers brakes, steering and suspension, wheels and tyres, body and glass, seats and seatbelts, lights, and leaks.  The most common fails are simple things: worn tyres, a light that doesn't work, pe

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Brakes
docs.a: The brake pedal and handbrake work properly, and the pedal doesn't sink to the floor under steady pressure. Brake parts you can see aren't leaking and are securely mounted. A brake test shows the car stops hard enough and in a straight line. The brake and ABS warning lights come on when you turn the key and go out once the engine is running. A brake or ABS light that stays on is a reason to fail.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Steering and suspension
docs.a: The steering wheel is secure and doesn't have too much free play. Steering parts under the bonnet and under the car are all there, tight, and not worn past the limits. Suspension parts aren't broken, cracked or loose, shock absorbers and struts work and are securely mounted, and the wheels don't have too much play when raised.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Wheels and tyres
docs.a: Every road tyre has at least 1.5mm of tread on the surfaces that touch the road. No deep cuts, bulges or exposed cords. Wheels aren't damaged, wheel nuts are all there, and nothing rubs on the tyres when you steer or go over bumps. Tyres are one of the easiest fails to see coming. Our summer car check explains how to read your tread.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Body, glass and seats
docs.a: Doors open, close and latch properly from inside and out. The windscreen in front of the driver isn't cracked or badly damaged. Window tint isn't darker than the rules allow. No rusted sharp edges on the outside, and no advanced rust or cracks in structural areas such as seat and seatbelt mounts. Rear vision mirrors are fitted and give a clear view. Seats are secure, and every seatbelt is there, isn't knotted, locks into its buckle and has a working retractor. Wipers and blades are in good condition, the horn works and the demister blows air onto the windscreen. If the car has airbags, the airbag warning light comes on at start-up and then goes out.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Lights
docs.a: Headlights on high and low beam, park lights, tail lights, brake lights, indicators and the number plate light all work. Lenses aren't broken so that white light shows where it shouldn't, and there are no tinted covers over lights. Headlights are aimed correctly and the reflectors aren't badly tarnished. The rear reflectors are fitted and undamaged.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Engine, exhaust and fuel
docs.a: No oil leaking from the engine, gearbox or driveline onto the road, the exhaust or the brakes. The exhaust is securely mounted, doesn't leak, and comes out behind the rear passenger doors. The fuel system doesn't leak. On LPG cars, the gas system gets its own set of checks. We cover those in pink slips for LPG and diesel cars .

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: What commonly fails a pink slip
docs.a: Plenty of fails aren't big mechanical problems. They're often small things that are easy to miss when you drive the car every day: tyres worn below 1.5mm, or worn unevenly on the inside edge where you can't see it. a blown globe, often a number plate light or a single brake light. split or smearing wiper blades. a brake, ABS or airbag warning light that stays on. an oil leak heavy enough to drip. a crack in the windscreen in the driver's view. a seatbelt that won't retract or latch. A five-minute walk around the car before you book can save a second trip. Turn on every light and get someone to stand behind the car while you press the brake.

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: What a pink slip doesn't check
docs.a: It's a safety check, not a full service or a pre-purchase inspection. It won't tell you when the timing belt is due, how healthy the engine is or whether the air con works. For that, a logbook service or a repair inspection is the better fit. If you're unsure whether you need a pink slip or a blue slip, read pink slip vs blue slip or try the walk-around pink slip check on our home page .

docs.t: Pink slip checklist NSW: what's checked: Common questions
docs.a: What is the minimum tyre tread for a pink slip in NSW? The NSW safety check standards reject a tyre with less than 1.5mm of tread on the surfaces that normally touch the road. Will a check engine light fail a pink slip? The standards list the brake, ABS and airbag warning lights. docs.t: Pink slip vs blue slip NSW: which one?: What a pink slip is
docs.a: A pink slip is the everyday name for a NSW safety inspection report. The NSW Government says most light vehicles more than five years old need one each year to renew their registration. The five years are counted from the month and year on the car's compliance plate. For imported vehicles, the count starts from the month and year of manufacture. So a car with a compliance plate dated March 2021 needs its first pink slip at the rego renewal after March 2026. The inspection is done at an Authorised Inspection Scheme (AIS) station. When the car passes, the station sends the result to Transport for NSW electronically, so there's no paper slip for you to post off. The report is valid for six months, and you need to renew your rego within that time. You can see what goes into the check in our plain-English pink slip checklist .

docs.t: Pink slip vs blue slip NSW: which one?: When you need a blue slip instead
docs.a: A blue slip covers safety and also confirms the car's identity. NSW requires one if your vehicle: has had its registration expired for more than three months. was brought into NSW from another state, territory or country. has no number plate. is a written-off vehicle that has been approved for re-registration. It may also be needed after significant changes, such as a new engine, or to clear some defect notices. A blue slip report is valid for 42 days from the date of inspection, so book it close to when you plan to register the car.

docs.t: Pink slip vs blue slip NSW: which one?: How to tell which one your car needs
docs.a: Start with your rego renewal notice. Service NSW says the notice states whether or not you need an inspection. If it does, and the car is already on NSW rego, that's a pink slip. If you've just bought a car from Queensland, imported one, or let the rego lapse for more than three months, you're in blue slip territory. If the rego expired less than three months ago, you can usually renew as normal, with a pink slip if the car is over five years old. Cars under five years old don't need a pink slip to renew. Some vehicles are exempt too, including some historic, conditionally registered and seasonally registered vehicles and some light trailers. The NSW safety checks page lists them.

docs.t: Pink slip vs blue slip NSW: which one?: What each one costs in NSW
docs.a: NSW sets the most an inspection station can charge. From 1 July 2026, the maximum fees for a light vehicle, including GST, are: pink slip (safety check): $52. blue slip (safety and identity check): $82. Motorcycles and trailers have their own, lower maximums. NSW reviews these fees each 1 July, so check the NSW fees page if you're reading this after June 2027.

docs.t: Pink slip vs blue slip NSW: which one?: If the car doesn't pass
docs.a: A failed check isn't the end of the road. If you have the repairs done within 14 days and take the car back to the same station to be reassessed, there's no extra inspection fee. After 14 days, you pay for another inspection. That's one reason to have the check done somewhere that also does repairs. If a worn tyre, a blown globe or a brake issue turns up, it can be looked at or booked in straight away.

docs.t: Air con, tyres, battery: summer checks: Air con: signs it needs a regas or repair
docs.a: It blows cool but not cold, or takes much longer to cool the car than it used to. Airflow is weak even on high, which can point to a blocked cabin filter. A musty or damp smell when you turn it on. A new rattle, squeal or clunk when the air con switches on. It cools for a while, then blows warm. What a regas is. Car air con works by pumping refrigerant gas around a sealed system. A regas removes what's left in the system, then refills it with the right amount and type of refrigerant for your car. The system is sealed, so if it's low on gas, there's usually a leak somewhere, even if it's slow. That's why a good air con job checks for leaks rather than just topping up. If a part like the compressor or a fan has failed, a regas alone won't fix it. The air con also helps clear a fogged windscreen, so take more care in wet weather until it's fixed.

docs.t: Air con, tyres, battery: summer checks: Tyres: signs they're worn
docs.a: Hot roads and full summer road trips are hard on tyres. Look for: Tread close to the wear bars. Most tyres have small raised bars across the bottom of the grooves. When the tread is level with them, the tyre is worn out. Uneven wear. One edge worn more than the other usually points to wheel alignment or suspension wear. Check the inside edge too, as it's easy to miss. Cracks, cuts or bulges in the sidewall or tread. A tyre that keeps losing pressure , or a tyre pressure light that keeps coming back. Vibration or pulling to one side at speed. For the pink slip, the NSW safety check standards fail a tyre with less than 1.5mm of tread on the surfaces that touch the road, or with deep cuts, bulges or exposed cords. Grip in the wet drops well before that point, so don't wait for the limit. Check your tyre pressures. Set them to the pressures on the tyre placard, often inside the driver's door, and check them when the tyres are cold. Low pressure makes a tyre run hotter and wear faster. Don't forget the spare.

docs.t: Air con, tyres, battery: summer checks: Batteries: signs it's on the way out
docs.a: Heat is hard on car batteries, and a battery weakened over summer often fails on the first cold morning. Watch for: the engine cranking slowly before it starts. a clicking sound and no start. headlights or dash lights dimming when you start the car. white or green crusting on the battery terminals. a swollen or cracked battery case. needing a jump start more than once. If your battery is several years old, have it tested before summer. A test checks how well it holds and delivers charge, so you replace it on your own terms rather than in a car park. Battery light or flat battery? A battery light on the dash while you're driving is a different problem. It usually means the battery isn't being charged, often because of the alternator, a drive belt or a wiring fault. The car may stop once the battery runs down, so switch off what you don't need and get somewhere safe. Our warning lights guide has more.
